title: A very present help (Psalm 46)
hookLine: though the mountains shake into the sea, God is our refuge
tomorrow: create in me a clean heart
last: WHY SO CAST DOWN, MY SOUL?

lines: A RIVER THAT SHOULDN'T BE THERE.
cards: Most phones have a place for an emergency contact: one name, for the moment something goes badly wrong. People don't usually pick the most impressive person they know.
They pick the one who picks up, the one who has shown up before, at two in the morning, at the side of the road. Psalm forty-six is a song about that kind of help.

Months ago on this path, you met one of its lines, be still. Today, the rest of the song: the earthquake that comes before the stillness, and a river that, on any map of Jerusalem, shouldn't be there.

teach.b: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." In King James English, very present means near at hand, right there.
The Hebrew says it a little differently: a help in troubles, found very much. Found again and again. Help with a track record.

"Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." Waters roar, mountains shake, nations rage. Nothing in this psalm pretends trouble isn't real.

teach.h: A RIVER IN A CITY WITHOUT ONE
teach.b: And right in the middle of the noise, verse four: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Here's the surprise. Jerusalem had no river.

It had a spring, the Gihon, and water carried through tunnels, but no river running through its streets. So the psalm sings one anyway. Some readers hear it as a picture of God's presence in the middle of his people.
Then verse five: God will help her, "and that right early."

teach.h: HELP AT THE TURNING OF MORNING
teach.b: In the Hebrew, that's at the turning of the morning. The help arrives as the night ends.

teach.h: THE LORD OF HOSTS IS WITH US.
teach.b: Twice the psalm repeats its chorus: "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge." And each time, one more word: Selah. Nobody knows for sure what it means.
One common guess is a pause in the music. If so, the pause falls right after the line about who's with us.

how: Some Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of disaster, war or fear, and it lies behind Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God."

games.why: verse 4: "there is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Jerusalem had no river. the psalm sings one into the middle of the storm.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that has been making your chest tight, and let it be there, like the roaring water, without fighting it or solving it.

Then look for the river: breathe in slowly, let the breath out longer than it came in, and feel where you're held up. If you pray, say the first verse once, slowly, God is our refuge and strength; if not, just keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Selah. The mysterious word that follows this psalm's refrain twice, maybe marking a pause in the music right after who is with us.

orig.note: Hebrew: help. the psalm calls God a help in troubles, "found very much": help with a track record.

carryVoice: Your line: found very much. Help that holds, even while the mountains shake. See you tomorrow.
